logical_blocks.content: Progressive Web Applications (PWA) are single-page applications that behave like traditional desk-top or mobile applications.  Although typically developed using JavaScript-based frameworks, Blazor presents an alternative approach using .NET technology. Blazor allows developers to build interactive web applications using C# instead of JavaScript, potentially offering new advantages for PWA develop-ment. However, the specific benefits and limitations of using Blazor for PWAs have not been explored.

This study aims to fill this gap by evaluating two functionally identical applications, one developed using Blazor and the other with Vue.js, a widely adopted JavaScript framework. The development pro-cess for both applications is described in detail, highlighting the architectural decisions, implementation challenges, and specific techniques used to meet the requirements of PWA. The applications were compared by initial load time, runtime performance, and application size.  In addition, the developer experience was measured by examining the volume of code and the startup time of the development server.

The findings show that Blazor with WebAssembly-based client-side rendering is a suitable option for developing PWAs, especially when performance is not the primary concern. It meets essential PWA requirements such as offline support, installability, and background synchronization.  It also provides advantages in development efficiency and maintainability by reducing the volume of code needed for application logic. However, its larger application size and performance trade-offs make it less suitable for performance-critical applications compared to frameworks like Vue.js. Keywords: Progressive Web Application, Blazor, Vue.js, WebAssembly, JavaScript frameworks, .NET

Over the last decade, we have seen significant changes in the field of web development, driven by advances in web frameworks, increased computer performance and bandwidth, and shifting user expectations. One of them started in 2015, when two Google employees, developer Alex Russell and designer Frances Berriman, introduced the concept of Progressive Web Applications (PWAs).  They saw PWAs as a way to bring the best user experiences from native mobile apps to the web by using features such as service workers and web app manifests. [1]

The usage and popularity of the new web application standard have increased significantly since it was introduced. Flipkart, India’s largest e-commerce platform, was one of the first to use this technol-ogy in their application, Flipkart Lite. This new application dramatically improved the user experience compared to the previous mobile platform. The adoption of the new standard resulted in users spend-ing three times more time on the website, a 40% higher reengagement rate, a 70% higher conversion rate among users who reached the site using the "Add to Homescreen" function, and a three times lower data usage.[2]

Other major companies have recognized the value of PWAs and have joined the trend. Platforms such as Twitter, Forbes, Alibaba, and many others benefited significantly, with lower data consumption, significant increases in conversions, monthly active users, as well as faster loading times and higher user sessions and engagement. [1]

The advantages of PWAs are not limited to large corporations, as they can offer significant benefits to startups by accelerating product development and reducing costs.  Unlike traditional native apps, they can be developed, tested, and deployed quickly, allowing startups to iterate through ideas cost-effectively.  This makes them a powerful tool for companies that want to accelerate the development of prototypes and effectively match product to market.  Using PWAs, startups can allocate resources more efficiently to innovation and refinement of their offerings, rather than investing heavily in native app development. [3]

Given the numerous benefits provided by PWA, the technology has been widely adopted since its introduction in 2015.  However, when deciding to adopt this web standard, developers face a crucial question: which framework and programming language to use?  Traditionally, JavaScript has been the main language for web development, and frameworks such as Angular, React, and Vue.js were designed to facilitate PWA creation. However, the web development environment is changing and new technologies are emerging that can provide attractive alternatives.

This thesis examines Blazor technology as one of the alternatives to JavaScript frameworks in PWA development. Blazor, a technology developed by Microsoft, is a modern front-end web framework that allows developers to create interactive web applications using mainly C# and .NET, while still allowing for integration with JavaScript.  It supports two hosting models: server-side and WebAssembly.  The server-side model performs application logic on the server and handles the user interface via a real-time SignalR connection, whereas Blazor WebAssembly runs code client-side in the browser on a WebAssembly-based .NET runtime. [4]

The purpose of this study is to investigate the suitability of using Blazor technology to implement progressive web applications.  The study covers the implementation of selected aspects of PWA in Blazor and compares them with a reference technology built on JavaScript, in particular Vue.js.  To achieve this goal, the study answers the following research questions: RQ1  What are the technical capabilities of Blazor in meeting PWA requirements? In the following, all the chapters included in the thesis are listed, together with a brief description:

Introduction - Provides background information on the thesis and its objectives.
State of the Art - Reviews existing literature on Blazor in the context of modern web develop-ment, identifying a gap in studies on its use for Progressive Web Applications and comprehensive evaluations of developer experience.
Progressive Web Application - Introduces the concept of Progressive Web Applications and covers essential PWA technologies such as the Web App Manifest, Service Workers, and HTTPS.
Blazor - Provides an in-depth look at the Blazor framework, particularly focusing on Blazor WebAssembly, which enables PWA implementation.  Describes how Blazor allows C# devel-opment in the browser and explores the structure and behavior of Blazor applications.
Vue - Presents Vue.js, chosen as the reference technology to compare how Blazor differs from a JavaScript framework in the context of PWA development. It discusses Vue’s rendering mecha-nisms, component system, and supporting build tools.
Development of Experimental Progressive Web Applications - Describes the implementa-tion of two equivalent PWA applications, one developed using Blazor and the other using Vue. Details the features, responsive design, service worker setup, and hosting configurations of both applications.
Comparison of PWA Implementations - Presents an analysis of the two applications in terms of initial load and runtime performance, size, volume of code, and development server startup time.

logical_blocks.content: In the thesis “WebAssembly Approach to Client-side Web Development using Blazor Frame-work“ [5] author compared the three most popular JavaScript frameworks to Blazor technology.  The comparison was performed by evaluating the learning curve of each technology, the size needed to be downloaded to the browser to ensure proper functionality of this framework, and the existence of de-veloper tools to support the creation of the application. According to the findings, the Blazor framework was moderately challenging to learn due to its architectural concepts, but easier to use than Angular, while it was more difficult than Vue.js. In terms of application size, Blazor got the worst score, requiring approximately five times more memory than React and Vue.js. A similar score was reached in compar-ison to ram usage, where Blazor was also ranked last.  However, it is important to note that the tests were conducted using a preview version of Blazor, and in the future, it may achieve better results and become a popular choice for web application development.

The thesis is not focused solely on comparing frameworks, dedicating only one chapter in which we will find a description of the achievements of the above-mentioned technologies. In the further part, the authors present detailed information about the architecture of Blazor Server and Blazor WebAssembly applications and describe how the development process in this technology looks like.

In the article "WebAssembly as an alternative to JavaScript in the development of modern web applications" [6], Blazor technology was used to investigate the potential of WebAssembly tech-nology in the development of web applications. As a benchmark for evaluating the performance of the Blazor application, a twin version of the application was developed using Angular.  The comparisons involved various aspects such as application loading time, data transfer size, duration of Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) requests handling, and difficulty of writing code. In addition, two separate im-plementations were prepared for testing purposes, focusing on measuring the execution time of sorting object lists and the generation of Document Object Model (DOM) elements.

The results showed that the Blazor performed worse than the Angular in almost all criteria tested. The size of the Blazor application was significantly larger than that of the Angular application.  This is due to the need to download the runtime environment, however, these data do not need to be downloaded every time the application loads since web browsers store them in a cache, significantly improving performance. As the initial loading time is influenced by the size of the application and the number of requests, this metric was also favorable for a JavaScript-based framework.  Furthermore, the results revealed that Blazor experienced longer delays in handling HTTP requests compared to Angular, as WebAssembly currently needs more direct HTTP operation capabilities.

Another experiment compared the performance of JavaScript, C++, Angular, and Blazor in sort-ing an n-element list of objects.  The results revealed a significant performance difference between JavaScript and WebAssembly, with C++ compiled into WASM performing operations significantly faster than equivalent JavaScript code. The performance of Angular remained comparable to that of a single script. However, regardless of collection size, Blazor performed significantly worse than Angular in the sorting test.

The authors also measured the performance of modifying the DOM elements in both applications. Compared to Angular, Blazor took much longer to add a thousand, three thousand, and ten thousand elements to the document tree. Because WebAssembly currently lacks direct access to the DOM tree, all Blazor modifications are carried out using generated JavaScript code, so delays were expected, similar to the HTTP operations.  The code metrics analyzed do not definitively indicate which frame-work requires less effort to implement the same functionality.  In terms of the logic layer, five Blazor components had fewer lines of code than the remaining five Angular components. Angular had fewer lines of code in seven components in the presentation layer, while both frameworks had one compo-nent with the same number of lines. It implies that the syntax of Angular may be more precise, resulting in more condensed code.

The authors assessed that Blazor demonstrates the potential of WebAssembly by enabling the cre-ation of functional single-page applications using a different approach to traditional JavaScript coding. Although WebAssembly can be an alternative to JavaScript, it does not replace it entirely, as certain browser functionalities can only be achieved through JavaScript.

Article “Modern Web Frameworks: A Comparison of Rendering  describes the rendering strategies used in Angular, React, Vue, Svelte and Blazor, which are the most popular web frameworks. All reviewed frameworks share a common goal: maintaining synchronization between the state of DOM and the state of the component tree by creating and updating the DOM nodes and their attributes.

The authors conducted various different benchmarks, and in each one they implemented an ap-plication identically with each framework and performed a particular action that measures the costs of a particular aspect of rendering by varying the size and shape of the component tree.  After each scenario, they meticulously measure the time taken for script execution in the render cycle. The bench-mark tests performed are used to compare the frameworks in terms of relative differences. The results are presented in absolute terms, measured in milliseconds, but the authors point out that the simplicity of the components used does not accurately reflect the expected performance of a real application with a component tree of equivalent size.

The results show that Blazor, being the only WebAssembly-based framework among the reviewed ones (Angular, React, Vue, and Svelte), exhibits significantly worse performance compared to its JavaScript-based counterparts, including React, which shares an identical rendering model. It is noted that this discrepancy in performance cannot definitively be attributed to factors specific to Blazor or inherent weaknesses in WebAssembly itself. However, the need to mediate access to DOM Applica-tion Programming Interface (API) through a JavaScript layer is identified as a factor contributing to the observed overhead in Blazor’s results.

Furthermore, the results indicate that frameworks such as Blazor, which lack the capability to auto-matically determine dirty components as provided by frameworks like Vue.js, experience performance challenges.  This can particularly affect small transitions and complex User Interfaces (UIs), which can lead to an unresponsive user experience. It is implied that such frameworks may require manual optimization efforts, which are automatically handled by other frameworks.

The existing literature focuses mainly on factors related to Single Page Applications (SPAs) and their development using Blazor. Nevertheless, the literature review lacks publications exploring the possibil-ities and advantages of employing the Blazor framework for developing Progressive Web Applications. PWAs are increasingly recognized as a contemporary approach to web application development, so investigating the potential of Blazor within this realm could offer valuable insights and perspectives to developers working with the .Net stack.

Furthermore, most existing studies focus mainly on performance metrics, offering only limited in-sight into the developer experience. Evaluations that utilize code metrics analyze the number of lines of code within components, which may not accurately reflect the effort involved in the development process. This highlights the need for a more in-depth assessment of the developer experience.

All reviewed publications are approximately three years old. Since then, the Blazor framework has undergone significant advances and improvements.  This provides an opportunity to provide a more up-to-date understanding of Blazor’s suitability for different application development scenarios.

The universal accessibility, strong security, and open standards of the Web make it an ideal platform to deliver software that anyone can access and share.  Web applications work on any device with a single codebase and are easy to deploy without the need for packaging, content reviews, or dealing with update delays.  Users are guaranteed to get the most recent version every time they access an application.[9]

In contrast, platform-specific applications offer deep integration with devices, enabling rich func-tionality and offline use.  However, they are often tied to specific platforms, making cross-platform compatibility challenging. Progressive Web Applications merge the strengths of both, combining the accessibility of web applications with the user experience similar to native applications.[9]

Progressive Web Applications (PWAs) are called "progressive" because they rely on a technique known as progressive enhancement.  This approach focuses on developing a core experience that works across all devices and browsers, while allowing for more advanced functionality on more capable devices. With progressive enhancement, every user has access to the application’s core functionality, regardless of device limitations.  However, as the device and browser engine’s capabilities increase, the application will be able to unlock new features and provide better performance. On more advanced devices, PWA may offer offline access, push notifications, or integration with hardware components such as the camera or GPS. [10]

Progressive enhancement is an important characteristic of Progressive Web Applications, but there are more factors that contribute to delivering a native app-like experience.  Google identified five es-sential criteria that also play a significant role in making a web application installable, reliable, and user-friendly on different devices and browsers.[11] Key aspects include:

Performance: A PWA should load quickly and maintain high performance throughout the user interaction. Fast loading is critical because slow page loads significantly increase the likelihood of user abandonment. Consistently smooth performance, including responsive interactions and animations, enhances the user experience.
Cross-browser compatibility: PWAs are fundamentally web applications, which means they must function across all browsers. A practical approach to achieving this is to first identify the core features and implement them using the most basic technology available. Once this foundational functionality is established, additional features and improvements can then be added.
Responsive design: It is important to note that devices vary in size and that users may interact with an application on different screens.  While the tasks that users need to complete and the content that they want to access remain constant, it is necessary to adjust and rearrange the content to ensure that it is accessible and functional on any viewport size.
Custom Offline Page: Instead of displaying the browser’s default offline page, a PWA should provide a custom offline page to maintain a consistent user experience when the user is offline.
Installability: PWAs should be installable, allowing users to add the application to their device’s home screen. This installation mimics the behavior of native apps, leading to increased engage-ment and improved user metrics such as repeat visits and longer sessions.[11]

logical_blocks.content: Although a PWA may include many different features, there are three technologies that are essential for an application to be considered a true progressive web application:

Web Application Manifest : This file is critical to making PWAs discoverable and installable. It contains important metadata, including the name of the application, launch Uniform Resource Locator (URL), icons, and other details needed to present the website as an app on users’ devices.
Service  : This is a technology that enables developers to intercept and manage network requests and asset caching within the web browser.  Service workers are key to creating fast, reliable web pages and enabling offline functionality, which are hallmarks of PWAs.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) : PWAs must be delivered over a secure server using HTTPS. The security provided by HTTPS is critical because many of the advanced features of PWAs, particularly the service workers, are only available over secure connections. [10]

logical_blocks.content: A Web Application Manifest is a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) file that provides metadata about a web application. This file is used by web browsers to allow users to install web applications on their devices. The manifest file allows the developer to define how their web app should appear to the user and provides the information necessary for adding it to the user’s home screen.
The manifest file is linked to the HyperText Markup Language (HTML) of the web app via a <link> tag situated within the <head> section of the document, as shown in the Listing 3.1. [12]
According to the manifest specification, all fields are optional. However, to meet the requirements for Progressive Web Apps, certain manifest members must be included, such as:

name or short_name
icons must contain a 192px and a 512px icon
start_url
display and/or display_override
prefer_related_applications must be false or not present [12]

Service workers are a technology that brings multiple capabilities to web applications.  The most significant of these is the ability to operate in scenarios where Internet connectivity is either limited or unavailable.  They function as proxy servers, situated between the web application, the browser, and the network.  This enables the app to perform tasks such as offline access, interception of network requests, caching of resources, and providing fallback content when the network is not accessible. [13]

A service worker is an event-driven background task, created via a script, that operates within a specific origin (the combination of protocol, domain, and port) and a defined path, which determines the scope of its control. It has the form of a JavaScript file that manages the associated web page by intercepting and modifying navigation and resource requests, and caching resources.  When an app requests a resource, it can serve it from the cache, fetch it from the network, or generate it locally, providing a platform-like experience even when offline. Running in a separate worker context, service workers are non-blocking, fully asynchronous, and operate on a different thread from the main app, ensuring they don’t interfere with primary processes.[13] [14]

In order to successfully implement service workers in PWAs, it is essential to gain an understanding of their lifecycle. This involves a number of distinct phases, which are illustrated in the Figure  3.1.
Figure 3.1: The lifecycle of service worker

The journey of a service worker begins with registration. When a user first opens the website, all network requests initially go directly to the server because the service worker hasn’t taken control yet. The registration process starts by checking if the browser supports the Service Worker API. Once this is confirmed, PWA registers the service worker script. The location of the script determines its scope; placing it at the root gives it control over the entire domain, while placing it in a subdirectory limits its scope. [14]

logical_blocks.content: After successful registration and installation, the service worker state changes to ’activating’. During the activation, tasks such as cleaning up old caches can be performed, which is important for service

worker updates. For a new service worker, activation occurs immediately after installation. Once activation is complete, the state changes to ’activated’. By default, a new service worker will only take control of the pages on the next navigation or page refresh.  This ensures that any currently active pages continue to function under the control of the previous service worker until they are reloaded. [16]

Service workers are designed to be resource efficient, which means that they run only when neces-sary. After performing their tasks, service workers enter an idle state. If there are no active clients within their scope, the service worker will be terminated by the browser after being idle for a few seconds or working too long, to conserve memory and Central Processing Unit (CPU) resources.  However, ser-vice workers are automatically restarted when needed, such as when a new network request occurs or a message is sent to them.  This ensures that service workers are available to perform necessary actions without consuming resources unnecessarily.[17]

Caching is a fundamental aspect of developing PWAs that enables them to be both fast and reliable and less dependent on network conditions. Service workers allow developers to cache specific assets independently of the main application thread, providing greater control over how and when resources are stored on users’ devices. However, this also brings with it the responsibility to use storage space and bandwidth wisely, as these assets are downloaded and stored locally.  The key is to achieve an optimal balance between caching enough assets to ensure a fast, reliable, or offline experience without overloading the user’s device with excessive data. [18]

To achieve fast load times, it is essential to cache the components required to render the user interface.  This typically includes the main page’s HTML, CSS stylesheets, images, JavaScript files, web fonts, etc. By caching these assets, PWA is able to rapidly display a fully functional interface. This process typically occurs during the Service Worker’s installation. [18]

In addition to these assets, providing an offline experience requires caching at least an offline page. This page informs users that they are offline and that certain requests cannot be completed at the moment. However, the offline experience can be further enhanced by caching interactive elements, allowing users to continue engaging with the app even without a network connection, for example, view-ing previously accessed content.This is possible by intercepting network requests in service workers on a fetch event.[10]
With the fetch event, there are different strategies for handling user requests:

Cache First: Resources are retrieved from the cache first, ensuring quick load times and a network fallback in case there is no matching request in the cache.
Network First: The strategy prioritizes the retrieval of the latest content from the network, making it ideal for frequently updated resources like articles and social media feeds, with a fallback to cached content in the event of a network failure. However, this approach can result in delays for users with slow or unreliable connections, as they must wait for the network request to time out before accessing cached content, which could lead to a frustrating experience.
Stale-While-Revalidate: The strategy serves cached content while simultaneously fetching up-dated content from the network, which is then stored in the cache for future use. This approach ensures that users have fast access to cached resources while keeping the cache up-to-date with the latest content in the background. Ideal for resources that change very often but where the newest version is not essential.[19]

logical_blocks.content: Another feature enabled by the service workers in PWAs that allows them to function like native applications is the ability to send push notifications.  The automatic delivery of push messages and notifications helps with re-engaging users and delivering new content as soon as it becomes available.

The implementation of push notifications is achieved through the collaboration of two distinct APIs: the Push API and the Notifications API. The Push API enables web applications to receive messages sent from a server, regardless of whether the application is in the foreground or even currently loaded on a user agent. This enables developers to deliver asynchronous notifications and updates to users who have consented to receive them. The Notifications API allows web pages to manage the display of system notifications to the user. These notifications appear outside the main browsing context, which means that they can be shown even when the user has switched tabs or moved to another app. [20]
To successfully deliver push notifications to the user, it is essential to understand the three key steps involved in the process:

Client-Side Subscription: The first step is to subscribe the user to receive push notifications. This involves asking the user for permission through the Notifications and Permissions APIs and then using the Push API to deliver a PushSubscription .  This is an object that contains all the necessary information to send a push message to the user’s device, including, inter alia, an end-point pointing to the user’s browser push service and the keys to encrypt the push message data. Once PushSubscription is obtained, it is sent to the backend server and stored in a database for future use.
Sending a Push Message: When the server wants to send a push message, it makes a Repre-sentational State Transfer (REST) API call to the endpoint of a push service. This push service is responsible for handling the request, managing the delivery of the message, and queueing it if the device is offline. The API call includes details such as the recipient’s information, the data to be sent, and specific instructions on how the message should be delivered, such as time-to-live and urgency levels. The push message data is encrypted, preventing push services from viewing it. This is a crucial aspect, as the browser determines which push service is used, which could potentially result in browsers employing a push service that is not secure.
Handling the Push Event:  Once the push service successfully delivers the message, the browser on the user’s device receives it, decrypts any data, and triggers a push event in the service worker.  The service worker may then perform a variety of tasks, including displaying a notification to the user, making analytics calls, or caching content for offline use.[21]

logical_blocks.content: PWAs are designed to function effectively even with unstable internet connectivity, so they need a mechanism to handle situations where users must interact with a server.  Background Sync offers a solution that allows tasks to automatically resume when connectivity is restored after a failed API call due to poor network conditions.

A chat app serves as a great example of utilizing this feature, where the user wants to ensure that their message is delivered.  In areas with unreliable connectivity, a regular web app might display a blank screen, a loading spinner, or an error message when trying to send a message. However, with Background Sync in PWA, you can still compose and send messages while offline. The app will queue these messages and automatically send them once the connection is reestablished.[22]

The implementation of Background Sync in an application begins by registering a sync event with a unique tag as shown in the Listing 3.3. The tag serves to identify the specific task that needs to be executed. [23]

Subsequently, the code to listen for the sync event must be added to the service worker. As demon-strated in Listing 3.4, when the sync event is triggered, the tag is checked, and if it matches, the do-SomeStuff() action is attempted. If the network is available, the sync event will complete successfully; if not, it will automatically retry using an exponential back-off strategy until it succeeds. [23]

Blazor is an open-source web framework developed by Microsoft as part of the .NET platform.  It has been designed to enable the creation of interactive web applications using C# and .NET Core as an alternative to JavaScript for front-end development.  Blazor applications are constructed with components, which are fundamental UI elements written as .NET C# classes that define dynamic UI rendering logic and manage user events.  Typically, they are implemented using a Razor syntax that combines C# and HTML markup in files with the .razor extension. [24]

Blazor is operating with two rendering modes: Client-Side Rendering (CSR) and interactive Server-Side Rendering (SSR). In SSR, user interactions and UI updates are handled through a real-time connection to the browser, established via SignalR. This technology employs WebSockets to transmit events and UI changes between the client and the server.  In CSR, WebAssembly is used to run C# code directly in the user’s browser, allowing each user to have their own local instance of the app. In contrast, Blazor Server operates with a single instance of the application on the server, to which multiple users connect simultaneously.[25]

With the release of .NET 8 in 2023, Blazor introduced interactive Auto (automatic) rendering, which enables the use of both server-side and client-side rendering within a single web application. Initially, the server-side ASP.NET Core runtime handles content rendering and interactivity.  Once the Blazor bundle is downloaded and the WebAssembly runtime is activated on the client, subsequent rendering and interactivity shift to the client side.  This approach typically offers the fastest app startup experi-ence.[26]

However, creating Progressive Web Applications with Blazor is only feasible by developing ap-plications that run entirely on WebAssembly in the browser, without involving a server.  Server-side rendering requires a stable network connection to maintain an active session between the user and the server, which conflicts with the offline functionality of PWAs. The standalone Blazor WebAssembly apps deploy assets as static files to a web server, and once downloaded, they can be cached and run offline as PWAs.[24]

WebAssembly is a type of code designed to run in modern web browsers, offering significant per-formance enhancements.  In contrast to JavaScript, which is the dominant language in web develop-ment, WebAssembly is not typically created manually. Instead, it functions as a compilation target for languages such as C++ or C# and others. This allows developers to execute code written in these lan-guages on the web at near-native speeds, enabling the creation of high-performance web applications that were previously impractical due to the limitations of JavaScript. [27]

As a high-level language, JavaScript can be resource-intensive to download, parse, and compile, which may lead to challenges in delivering a smooth user experience on devices with limited comput-ing power, especially for more demanding use cases.  WebAssembly uses binary format files which are smaller than equivalent files containing JavaScript code, reducing the time required for network downloads. Additionally, because the WebAssembly code is precompiled, it can be executed directly by a browser.  These features lead to improved performance, enabling faster loading and execution. As a result, WebAssembly enables the development of advanced web applications such as 3D games, virtual and augmented reality, complex image and video processing, and more.[27]

WebAssembly is platform independent, which means it will run the same code on any device with a compatible browser, regardless of operating system or hardware architecture.  It runs in a secure, sandboxed environment separate from the host machine.  This reduces the possibility of malicious code interacting with the system outside its intended boundaries.[27]

To understand how the applications written in C#, after compilation into WebAssembly, are fully ex-ecuted in a browser, it is important to know the initial process behind starting the Blazor WebAssembly application.

The startup process begins with the initial page load.  The browser sends a GET request to the server to fetch the main page of the Blazor WebAssembly application, which is typically a static in-dex.html file.  The browser then parses HTML and loads linked resources such as CSS, JavaScript, and images.  During this process, the browser initially renders the static HTML, displaying a place-holder, where the Blazor application will later render its content.[28]

As the Blazor WebAssembly initialization begins, the blazor.webassembly.js script is loaded and executed.  This JavaScript file handles the loading and initialization of the Blazor application within the browser.  First, it downloads the configuration file, blazor.boot.json , which contains a list of all required framework and application files.  These include .NET assemblies and the dotnet.wasm file, which is a complete .NET runtime compiled into WebAssembly binary format.  After downloading all the listed resources, the WebAssembly .NET runtime is initialized, loading the Blazor framework and the application. At this point, the application runs entirely in the client’s browser. [28]

The role of the blazor.webassembly.js script does not end with the loading and initialization of the Blazor application.  This part of the framework is crucial for performing the necessary DOM updates and providing APIs for scenarios requiring JavaScript interoperability.  The use of JavaScript in these scenarios is necessary due to WebAssembly’s limitations, as it cannot directly manipulate the DOM or interact with Web APIs. Although future advancements in WebAssembly may reduce the dependency on this file, at this moment it is essential for UI changes. [25]

When a user initiates a UI update, such as navigating from one page to another, the event is in-tercepted by Blazor’s JavaScript runtime (blazor.webassembly.js), which communicates with the Blazor framework running in the WebAssembly runtime (dotnet.wasm). The Blazor router processes the nav-igation request by identifying the corresponding component, creating an instance of it, and executing its lifecycle methods. [25]
During this process, Blazor constructs a Render Tree, which serves as an internal representation

of the UI structure of the component. To optimize updates, Blazor employs an incremental DOM approach.  Instead of re-rendering the entire UI, it compares the newly generated Render Tree with the previous one to determine the minimal set of required changes.  This comparison results in a

differential render tree that identifies elements that need to be added, updated, or removed. The calculated updates are then sent back to the JavaScript runtime, which applies them to the actual DOM. [29]

Vue.js was selected as the reference technology to examine how Blazor differs from a widely used JavaScript framework in the development, performance, and capabilities of Progressive Web Applica-tions. Released by software developer Evan You in 2014, Vue.js is an open-source framework that has gained significant popularity. Built on standard HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, Vue.js offers a declarative, component-based programming model that enables the efficient development of user interfaces of any complexity.[30]

Vue.js uses a template syntax that extends standard HTML that declaratively describes the HTML output based on the application’s JavaScript state.  The framework’s reactivity system automatically tracks changes in the state and efficiently updates the Document Object Model when modifications occur.  Similarly to Blazor’s use of .razor files, Vue.js encapsulates each component within a file with .vue extension, which contains the logic, template, and styles in a single unit.[30]

Components can be written in two different API styles: Options API and Composition API. The Options API, which was the original way to define components, organizes component code by options such as data, methods, and computed properties.  The Composition API, introduced in Vue 3, pro-vides an alternative way of defining component logic using functions, which can be more suitable for organizing complex logic and promoting code reuse.[30]

Vue.js, like other popular JavaScript frameworks, supports TypeScript.  TypeScript is a strongly typed programming language that builds on JavaScript and helps detect common errors through static analysis at build time, reducing the likelihood of runtime errors in production. It also makes refactoring code in larger applications more reliable and enhances the developer experience with type-based auto completion in Integrated Development Environment (IDE).[31]

Vue.js rendering mechanism utilizes the Virtual DOM concept, which serves as an in-memory repre-sentation of the UI. Instead of inefficiently manipulating the real DOM directly, Vue.js creates lightweight JavaScript objects called virtual nodes that mirror the structure of actual DOM elements. When the ap-plication’s state changes, Vue.js re-renders the Virtual DOM to produce a new virtual tree.  Then it efficiently compares this new tree with the previous one to identify the minimal set of changes needed. This process allows Vue.js to update only the parts of the real DOM that have changed, significantly optimizing performance.[32]

Vue.js currently uses Vite as its default build tool.  Vite is a modern build tool developed by the Vue team, designed to provide a faster and more efficient development experience, offering an op-timized workflow for both development and production builds.  Unlike traditional bundlers, Vite takes advantage of native ECMAScript Modules (ESM), making it possible to deliver an optimized workflow for development builds.[33]

Vite improves the development phase by enhancing dev server start times and optimizing module handling.  It separates modules into dependencies and source code: dependencies are pre-bundled using the fast "esbuild" tool since they change infrequently, accelerating initial load times. The source code is served over native ESM, allowing the browser to handle module loading and transform code on demand, reducing unnecessary processing. Vite enhances Hot Module Replacement by precisely updating only the changed modules, keeping updates fast regardless of application size and preserving application state without full page reloads.  It also utilizes browser caching through HTTP headers to minimize server requests during reloads. By offloading tasks to the browser and minimizing processing, Vite maintains high performance even as the application grows, resulting in a faster and more efficient development experience.[33]

For the production build, bundling is still used because unbundled ESM can be inefficient due to extra network round trips from nested imports, even with HTTP/2.  Bundling optimizes performance through tree-shaking, lazy-loading, and chunk splitting for better caching.  Vite uses Rollup 1 for this process because it offers a more flexible plugin API, which fits Vite’s infrastructure better than esbuild, despite esbuild’s faster performance.[33]

The goal of this chapter is to explore the development of two Progressive Web Applications, both with identical functionality but built using different technologies. logical_blocks.content: To support the primary objective of evaluating the PWA development process, the following PWA features were implemented in the DartPointTracker application:

Installability DartPointTracker supports installability by incorporating a Web App Manifest file.  This file in-cludes key metadata such as the application name, start URL, icons, and description. By provid-ing this information, the browser can detect the app as a PWA and prompt users to install it on their devices. This enables users to launch the app directly from their home screen, offering an experience similar to that of a native application. The application runs in a standalone window, removing the standard browser UI elements to further enhance this native-like behavior.
Offline Functionality The application provides extensive offline capabilities, allowing the core functions to be accessed without an Internet connection. Game logic and scorekeeping operations are handled locally on the device, allowing users to start new games and track scores without network access.  Com-pleted games are stored on the user’s device and synchronized with the server when connectivity is restored, ensuring the data is up to date. Upon synchronization, player statistics and Elo rank-ings are updated automatically, and users are notified once the synchronization is complete. Although most of the core features are accessible offline, there are some limitations.  Creating new players requires an internet connection to prevent duplicate names, and users are notified to go online for this action. Additionally, player rankings may not reflect the latest updates when offline, as cached data is displayed until the user reconnects, at which point the rankings are refreshed.
Responsive Design DartPointTracker implements responsive design principles to ensure that the user interface func-tions effectively on various devices and screen sizes. The layout automatically adapts to different screen resolutions and orientations, providing a consistent experience on both mobile devices and desktop computers.
Secure Context The application is served over HTTPS, ensuring a secure environment for users.  This secure context is essential for enabling features such as service workers and offline functionality.

The manifest contains all the essential fields required for the browser to allow app installation. The "display" property is specifically set to "standalone," which enables the application to open and function similarly to a native standalone app. This setting ensures that the app launches in a separate window with its own icon in the app launcher, and browser UI elements such as the URL bar are excluded.

For the development of service workers, the Workbox library was used to simplify the implementa-tion of caching strategies, background sync, and offline capabilities.

The Vue version of DartPointTracker benefits from a PWA plugin that is pre-configured with Work-box. This plugin automatically handles the integration of Workbox, allowing the service worker to utilize Workbox modules without requiring additional setup for module bundling. The custom service worker code in both applications can be divided into four main parts: updating the service worker, precaching assets, handling background synchronization, and runtime caching of API calls.

The code in Listing6.4 ensures that updates to the service worker take effect immediately.  The self.skipWaiting() function forces the newly installed service worker to become active immediately, by-passing the default waiting period. While this makes the new service worker active, it does not auto-matically mean that currently loaded clients (open pages) are controlled by it. Instead, it ensures that any new clients will use this version of the service worker moving forward.

To address currently open clients, the clientsClaim() function is then called. This ensures that the active service worker immediately takes control of all existing pages within its scope, without requiring users to manually reload those pages.

The cleanupOutdatedCaches() function adds an event listener to the service worker’s activate event, which is responsible for cleaning up old, incompatible caches created by previous versions of Workbox.  This ensures that outdated cache data is removed, freeing up storage space, and preventing conflicts with the updated version of the service worker.

The precacheAndRoute(self.__WB_MANIFEST) function precaches assets listed in the precache manifest, which replaces the placeholder variable self.__WB_MANIFEST in the service worker. It per-forms two key tasks:

Precaching : It adds the specified assets to the precache list, removing any duplicates, and stores the files in the cache during the service worker’s installation phase.
Routing : It automatically registers a fetch event listener that responds to network requests with the precached assets. If a request matches a file in the precache, the service worker serves the cached version. For requests that are not in the precache, the fetch event falls through to other fetch event listeners or network requests, allowing the app to handle uncached resources.[34]

The code in the Listing6.6 above registers a route for GET requests to URLs that begin with /Play-ers. This route uses Workbox’s NetworkFirst strategy, which prioritizes fetching fresh player data from the network whenever the user is online. To evaluate and compare the implementation of Progressive Web Applications using Blazor and Vue.js, both versions of the DartPointTracker application were deployed in a live environment.  This deployment is necessary to test key aspects, such as performance, user experience, and offline func-tionality under real-world conditions, ensuring accurate analysis of application behavior when accessed over the Internet.

The Firebase platform was selected as the hosting solution for both applications.Firebase provides a simple deployment process via the CLI interface, so updates can be quickly deployed with a single command (firebase deploy).  It also offers automatic Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) certificates, which are necessary for the functionality of the service worker, ensuring that both applications meet HTTPS requirements. [35]

Hosting both applications on the same platform ensures consistency in the testing environment. Any observed differences in performance, behavior, or user experience can be attributed to the frame-works, rather than to differences in hosting infrastructure or server configuration.

The objective of this study is to explore the feasibility of using Blazor technology to implement Progressive Web Applications.  In the previous chapter, the feasibility of implementing the core PWA features with Blazor was demonstrated, including service worker integration, asset precaching, offline functionality, installability, and background synchronization. The DartPointTracker application success-fully incorporated these features, confirming that Blazor meets the technical requirements for PWA development.

This chapter focuses on the second research question: What are the advantages and disadvan-tages of using Blazor to build PWAs in comparison to JavaScript-based technologies? To answer this, we will compare the performance and developer experience of building the DartPointTracker applica-tion in Blazor and Vue.js. The performance comparison will cover key metrics such as First Contentful Paint, Largest Contentful Paint, Total Blocking Time, and Speed Index for the first-time and repeat-visit experience. Furthermore, differences in storage usage for cached assets will be examined, along with the rendering performance of each application when processing requests from the API.
The developer experience will be evaluated by comparing the complexity and volume of code,

measured in lines of code, and a comparison of development server startup times. This analysis will provide insights into how Blazor compares to Vue.js in terms of both performance and ease of implementation, offering a comprehensive understanding of Blazor’s suitability for PWA development relative to JavaScript-based technologies.

The performance evaluation using Google Lighthouse highlights significant differences between Blazor WebAssembly and Vue.js PWAs concerning initial load metrics.  The data reveal that Blazor consistently underperforms compared to Vue on key performance indicators, particularly in the LCP and TBT, especially in mobile conditions.

Blazor WebAssembly applications require the download and initialization of the .NET runtime, ap-plication binaries, and dependencies before rendering any meaningful content.  This initial overhead contributes to longer load times and increased TBT, as the main thread remains occupied with pro-cessing these resources. For first-time visitors with clear storage, Blazor recorded an average LCP of approximately 12,989 ms and a TBT of 4,272 ms on mobile devices. In comparison, Vue achieved an LCP of 1,546 ms and a TBT of 35 ms under the same conditions.  The significant performance gap is more noticeable on mobile devices, where limited computational power and slower network speeds amplify the latency involved in downloading and initializing Blazor’s larger payload.

Asset caching significantly improves nearly all performance metrics for both applications by reduc-ing the need to download resources on repeated visits. In the case of Blazor, the LCP time decreases with caching because essential assets like the .NET runtime and application binaries are loaded from the local cache rather than fetched over the network. This reduction in network latency allows the main content to render more quickly, thus improving the LCP metric.

However, despite the improvement in LCP the TBT values are nearly identical on both device types, whether caching is enabled or not. This persistent high TBT is due to the computational overhead as-sociated with Blazor’s runtime initialization, which is not mitigated by caching. The main thread remains heavily occupied with parsing, compiling, and executing the WebAssembly modules and initializing the .NET runtime environment.  These CPU-intensive tasks block the main thread for extended periods, preventing it from responding to user interactions promptly and contributing to the high TBT metrics.

Vue.js applications outperform Blazor in terms of Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Total Blocking Time (TBT), and Speed Index. This is primarily due to Vue’s lightweight architecture and its use of the browser’s native JavaScript engine, eliminating the need for additional runtimes. As a result, Vue.js ap-plications benefit from quicker parsing and execution of scripts, leading to lower LCP and TBT values. For instance, with caching enabled on mobile devices, Vue.js achieved an LCP of 255 ms and a TBT of 62 ms, significantly outperforming Blazor in these metrics. Additionally, Vue.js exhibits lower Speed Index values, reflecting its efficiency in rendering content rapidly and providing a smoother visual pro-gression during page load.

Although Blazor shows slightly better results in First Contentful Paint (FCP), this advantage is largely attributed to the immediate display of a loading animation embedded directly in the index.html file, which is registered as the FCP. However, this early visual feedback does not translate to faster rendering of the main content.

Based on the results we can observe that Vue consistently outperforms Blazor in API request handling, with Vue processing requests up to 40 times faster. When making HTTP requests from We-bAssembly, the calls must traverse the WebAssembly-JavaScript boundary, since network access is controlled by the browser’s JavaScript environment.  Blazor’s HTTP client implementation adds addi-tional abstraction layers over browser fetch APIs that introduce performance overhead compared to Vue’s direct JavaScript approach.

Sort and rank assignment times remain relatively similar for both frameworks with smaller data sets, but Vue starts to show slower performance as the number of players increases. For 5,000 players, Vue’s sort time is actually higher than Blazor’s, indicating WebAssembly’s advantage in computational tasks that do not involve DOM manipulation or framework-specific operations.

The most significant performance difference is observed in the UI diffing phase, where Vue com-pletes the process significantly faster than Blazor. Vue’s diffing algorithm processes changes 30 times faster for 100 players, and this difference increases to 38 times faster for 5000 players, where the UI diffing phase takes nearly three seconds in Blazor.  Both frameworks perform UI diffing by com-paring the new UI representation with the previous state, but their approaches differ fundamentally. Blazor constructs a Render Tree and executes its diffing algorithm within the .NET runtime running on WebAssembly, which then requires communication of DOM updates across the WebAssembly-JavaScript boundary.  In contrast, Vue employs a Virtual DOM diffing approach that operates entirely within JavaScript, benefiting from modern JavaScript engine optimizations and avoiding the additional
overhead caused by boundary-crossing operations. This difference in execution environment con-tributes to the performance gap observed between the two frameworks.

Both frameworks appear to compute the minimal set of UI changes with similar accuracy, as evi-denced by the comparable rendering times observed in the browser rendering phase. The data show that rendering times remain relatively consistent between Vue and Blazor across all dataset sizes, indi-cating that both frameworks are generating similar sets of DOM operations for the browser to process.

The primary factor influencing the line count differences between Blazor and Vue implementations is Blazor’s use of dependency injection for HttpClient configuration.  It eliminates the need to repeatedly specify the API URL and authorization headers across all service methods. More configuration is needed in the SendGame method in Vue.  A method must be explicitly set to define the request as POST with a header that specifies the request body as application/json . Furthermore, JSON serialization must be handled manually using JSON.stringify() .  In contrast, Blazor’s PostAsJsonAsync automatically applies the necessary headers and serialization, reducing the verbosity.

The most significant difference in LOC is observed in the GetPlayers method. Vue requires error checking to confirm a successful request, followed by manual parsing with await  response.json() and mapping each object to a Player instance. In Blazor, GetFromJsonAsync simplifies this process by fetching data and automatically deserializing the JSON response into a list of Player objects in a single line. Any unsuccessful request triggers an HttpRequestException , which is handled within a try-catch block, eliminating the need for additional response validation.

The evaluation focused on the core domain classes, Player, Game and GameService, which contain the core business logic of the appli-cation. The analysis demonstrates clear differences in the volume of code between the Blazor (C#) and Vue (TypeScript) implementations. The Blazor version requires fewer lines of code, and the number of characters per line remains comparable in both implementations. This indicates that the code volume is significantly higher in the TypeScript implementation. The primary factors contributing to this outcome are as follows:

Primary Constructor: This is a syntax introduced in C# 12 that allows a constructor to be de-fined directly in the declaration of type and whose parameters are available anywhere in the body of type.[40] This allows the initialization of a property to be combined with its declaration. In contrast, in TypeScript, properties must be declared before the constructor, and the constructor method must explicitly assign each parameter to the corresponding property, resulting in numer-ous assignment statements that increase code length.
“this” Keyword: TypeScript requires explicit “this” references for every property and method access within class methods.  This requirement adds extra characters to nearly every line of operational code within class methods. In C#, the “this” keyword is optional in most contexts, as class members can be accessed directly by name without self-reference.
Collection Operations: C# makes use of LINQ expressions, which provide a declarative SQL-like syntax for collection operations.  These expressions are often more readable and concise than TypeScript’s approach using array methods like filter , map  and reduce .
Collection Indexing: C# simplifies accessing elements from the end of a collection with the caret  ^  operator, while TypeScript uses the collection’s length, resulting in longer expressions.
Computed Properties:  C# simplifies computed properties with expression-bodied members ( =>  avoiding the function blocks, braces, and return statements needed in TypeScript getters.

Program.cs in Blazor has more LOC than main.ts in Vue, where the difference is that they have different responsibilities. The Blazor file initializes the application by configuring the host builder, setting up dependency injection, and defining the HTTP client with api url and basic authentication.  It also specifies the root components and then runs the Blazor WebAssembly application. Meanwhile, the Vue file focuses on importing Bootstrap, configuring the router and store, and creating the Vue application instance. It then mounts the application to the DOM by targeting the #app element.

Table 7.15: Overall LOC Comparison Between Blazor and Vue

The overall results show that while the HTML markup requirements are similar between the two frameworks, there is a notable difference in the application logic implementation.  Vue consistently requires approximately 20-30% more lines of code across the presentation logic, infrastructure, and domain layers. Although this difference may not be significant for a relatively simple application, it could lead to increased development effort and maintenance challenges in larger, more complex projects.

A key factor contributing to this difference is that Blazor benefits from using C#, which often allows for more concise code compared to TypeScript. Although Blazor applications come with a larger initial download size due to .NET assemblies, these assemblies provide features not available in TypeScript, enabling developers to implement the same functionality with fewer lines of code.

The application startup layer is the only area where Vue demonstrates an advantage.  This differ-ence can be attributed to the architectural distinctions between the frameworks. Blazor’s startup code configures its dependency injection container, which, while requiring more initial setup, helps eliminate repetitive service configuration code throughout the application.

This analysis was conducted to evaluate the development experience by comparing the startup times of the development servers for Blazor and Vue. To ensure a consistent and automated evalua-tion, a Bash script was developed. The script records a timestamp before executing the command to start the development server. Then it streams the command output to a file and repeatedly checks the logs at 0.1 second intervals for a message indicating that the server has successfully started.  Once this log entry is identified, a second timestamp is recorded and the startup duration is calculated as the difference between the two timestamps. Using this script, ten measurements were taken for each framework. This approach provides an approximate measurement of the startup times of the develop-ment server. The results are presented in Table7.16.
Table 7.16: Development server startup times (ms) for Blazor and Vue

The results show that Vue’s development server starts significantly faster than Blazor’s after the initial run, with a median startup time of just 2.08 seconds compared to Blazor’s 10.16 seconds. The exception is Vue’s first run, which takes 15.3 seconds due to initial dependency resolution, pre-bundling operations, and cache creation. Once these tasks are completed, Vue’s startup performance stabilizes at a consistently faster level for all subsequent runs. The performance gap is primarily due to Vue’s use of Vite as its build tool and development server.  Vite employs an unbundled development approach, leveraging native ES modules in the browser to compile only the necessary files on demand rather than processing the entire application at startup.

Blazor, on the other hand, must initialize the complete .NET runtime environment before the appli-cation can start. Additionally, Razor components must be compiled into .NET assemblies, introducing further overhead.  Unlike Vue, which runs directly in the browser using JavaScript, Blazor requires a more complex initialization process, which results in longer startup times.

This study examined the suitability of using Blazor technology for the implementation of Progres-sive Web Applications and compared it with a JavaScript-based framework, Vue.js.  To achieve this, the research focused on two key questions: the technical capabilities of Blazor in meeting PWA re-quirements and the advantages and disadvantages of using Blazor in comparison to JavaScript-based technologies.

The findings of this study indicate that Blazor technology enables the development of Progres-sive Web Applications through its WebAssembly-based implementation, which runs entirely within the browser.  Essential PWA features including installability, offline access, and background synchroniza-tion, were successfully implemented in both applications developed during this research.  Although Blazor primarily supports C# development, it provides interfaces to execute JavaScript code when necessary, such as requesting notification permissions.

While Blazor includes a default PWA template with basic service worker implementation for offline access, this research evaluated Blazor’s compatibility with the widely adopted Workbox library, which simplifies service worker development.  The integration process revealed differences between frame-works: Vue.js offers a dedicated plugin with native Workbox compatibility, enabling automatic service worker generation, whereas Blazor requires manual integration by importing Workbox from a Content Delivery Network and utilizing Workbox CLI for precaching implementation. Despite these procedural differences, the service worker was successfully implemented within the Blazor framework.

Beyond the implementation of the service worker, other aspects of Blazor must be evaluated when considering its suitability for PWA development. The most significant challenge of using this technology is its performance. Blazor WebAssembly applications require downloading the .NET runtime and nec-essary dependencies before execution, resulting in a larger application payload. This leads to longer startup times compared to JavaScript frameworks such as Vue.js, which are optimized for fast initial rendering. The delay is especially noticeable on lower-end devices or under poor network conditions, where extended loading times can negatively impact the user experience.

In addition to load-time concerns, Blazor WebAssembly presents further runtime performance con-siderations. Although it enables the execution of C# code directly in the browser, WebAssembly can-not directly manipulate the DOM. Instead, UI changes must be captured by JavaScript, passed to WebAssembly where the C# code is executed, and then returned to JavaScript.  This architectural approach introduces overhead compared to Vue’s direct DOM manipulation. However, in pure compu-tational tasks, such as sorting datasets analyzed in this research, Blazor gains an advantage as the size of the dataset increases.

The difference in performance is also noticeable during the development process. Blazor’s server startup is more time consuming than Vue’s, due to the need to initialize the .NET runtime, compile Ra-zor components, and configure dependency injection. In contrast, Vue benefits from Vite’s lightweight, module-based compilation process, enabling faster startup and a more responsive development work-flow.

The main advantage of using Blazor for PWA development is its ability to significantly reduce overall code volume, resulting in a simpler and more maintainable codebase.  Using C# for application logic allows developers to write more concise code. The built-in dependency injection framework simplifies service configuration by eliminating redundancy, and the convention-based routing system automati-cally generates routes from the project structure, eliminating the need for separate routing configuration files. In the application developed for this research, these features reduced the number of code lines by 20–30% compared to Vue.

Based on the findings in this study, Blazor WebAssembly is a suitable option for PWA development in scenarios where performance is not the primary concern. Blazor fully meets all PWA requirements, providing features such as offline support, background sync, and installability. Although its larger ap-plication size and DOM updates across the WebAssembly-JavaScript boundary impact performance sensitive applications, it offers significant advantages in development efficiency and maintainability. It is especially suitable for teams already experienced with .NET, allowing developers to work within a familiar environment and reducing the learning curve.  Using C# for front-end applications simplifies code maintenance and ensures better long-term support, making it practical for in-house applications where rapid development and ease of maintenance take priority over performance requirements.

Future studies could explore several important areas to deepen the understanding of Blazor’s po-tential in PWA development.  Although this study compared the volume of code between Blazor and a Vue.js for a relatively simple application, examining larger and more complex projects could offer greater insight into how each technology manages scalability, maintainability, and project structure.

Another valuable direction for future research involves the security aspects of Blazor PWAs, with a particular focus on user authentication and authorization. This could include evaluating Blazor’s sup-port for modern protocols such as OAuth and OpenID Connect, and comparing these implementations with those used in JavaScript-based PWAs.  Additionally, it would be beneficial to assess how Blazor handles secure token management, permission scoping, and session persistence, especially in offline scenarios.

Furthermore, with the release of .NET 8, Blazor introduced an interactive auto rendering mode designed to improve initial load times by starting with server-side rendering and transitioning to We-bAssembly once the necessary client-side resources are loaded.  Although this approach currently lacks support for PWA development, future enhancements may introduce such capabilities.  If PWA support is introduced in the future, it would provide an important area for research, especially to under-stand its impact on startup performance and how mixed rendering modes work with key PWA features.
